newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Euro-MPs flex investigative muscles over BSE.
newsitem.headline: Euro-MPs flex investigative muscles over BSE.

text.p: The European Parliament flexed some new-found muscles on Tuesday as it launched an inquiry into the European Union's handling of the mad cow disease crisis.

Nineteen Euro-MPs, sitting as a temporary committee of inquiry, will consider whether the European Commission and certain EU states correctly informed the public about alleged dangers from bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE).

They will also investigate whether the EU is efficiently monitoring its global ban on exports of British beef and adopting adequate measures for protecting public health and restoring the smooth operation of the beef market.

European Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler and Irish Farm Minister Ivan Yates, representing the EU presidency, were to be the first to address the committee, which has been asked to issue a report by November 17.
The panel was expected to seek information from the Commission concerning allegations it sought to put market concerns above those of consumers.

Liberation, the French daily newspaper, reported on Monday that a senior Commission official had suggested in a memorandum in 1993 that EU veterinary experts avoid discussing the risk to humans posed by the disease.

It was the second such accusation concerning Commission policy. The Commission has denied trying to cover up any BSE dangers, pointing as proof to its speedy banning of British beef after evidence of a possible link between BSE and a deadly human equivalent.
The parliament's power to investigate comes courtesy of the Maastricht Treaty, which gave the EU assembly the right to probe alleged violations or maladministration of European Union law.
It has powers of inquiry similar to those of the EU's judicial bodies but cannot investigate matters that are already being dealt with by the EU or national courts.

The parliament set up its first committee of inquiry last December to look into alleged customs fraud in the EU's transit system, which the European Court of Auditors says is cheating the EU budget of nearly $250 million a year.
